content.thinking:
I'm thinking of a League of Legends glow-kit style scythe, roughly 2m haft with a 0.9m blade, displayed upright on a small stone plinth so it reads clearly rather than lying flat.

I'll plant the scythe vertically into a dark stone plinth with a rune ring, letting the curved blade sweep outward with floating soul-wisps drifting around it. For joints, I'll add a root at the plinth plus a hinge for a hanging soul-lantern charm so its chain can swing naturally.

The design concept is a dragonbone scythe: a haft built from stacked vertebrae with spiny processes, topped by a dragon skull that cradles the blade emerging from its jaws, with a crescent soul-glow edge in spectral teal against ivory bone and dark indigo metal with gold trim. Now I'm working out the precise geometry, planning the haft's curve and dimensions in meters along the upright plane.

Now I'm sizing the piece: a plinth base on the floor with the haft rising from it, overall height around 2.1 meters, with the blade sweeping perpendicular from the top of the haft and curving downward toward the tip in classic scythe fashion.

Writing blade curve coordinates...

Let me work out the centerline arc for the blade: picking a circle center below the haft and sweeping the angle from about 88° down to 35° gives a tip position around (0.82, -0.33), yielding a curved scythe-like blade length of roughly 0.92 units.

Now I'm shaping the width profile—wide at the base around 0.2 and tapering to a point, with a slight convex curve so the spine thickens near the root. I also want to add a small backward heel projection behind the haft, like a little swept spur on the spine side, to give the blade a dragon-wing silhouette.

I'm picturing the main blade as an ivory dragon-claw or horn shape with ridged grooves, plus a smaller secondary spike sweeping back like a wing-finger for silhouette interest. I also want a thin glowing teal crescent running along the inner cutting edge as a spectral highlight, and maybe dark-metal inlay runes on the blade face using decal or overlay extrusion since true cut-out holes aren't possible with simple extrusion.

Now I'm settling on the material design: a dark soulsteel blade with beveled edges mounted on a ribbed ivory bone spine, a glowing teal soul-gem at the base, and rune textures applied via small flat plane overlays positioned on the flat face of the blade since a curved SVG texture can't wrap the extrusion directly.

Still working out the glowing crescent edges and rune placement...

For the blade's surface paint, I'm planning a gradient from dark indigo at the spine to a bright violet-teal near the edge, hand-painted LoL style, with an added highlight streak for shine.

For the dragonbone haft, I'm aiming for an aged ivory look with grain texture and mottled yellowish shading, using tones like weathered bone and dark crevices, and considering how to render each vertebra segment along the shaft.

Designing vertebra lathe profiles...

Mid-grip gets a dark leather wrap with gold rings and a teal cord, plus spiral paint stripes and hanging soul-charm tassels—no vertebrae there. I'm laying out vertebra counts for the lower and upper haft sections with small cartilage-gap discs between each spool, then moving to the top where a stylized dragon skull cradles the blade root.

I'm figuring out the skull's orientation—facing +Z toward the viewer for readability, with horns sweeping outward like a crown and glowing teal eye sockets, while the blade attaches through a bone collar above the last vertebra around y=1.72–1.98.

I'm placing the cranium at y=1.80 and routing the haft upward through a cervical bone-neck that continues behind/above the skull to y=1.98, where the blade root plate attaches, then working out the total height including the drooping blade tip.

Total height lands around 2.15m, matching a typical scythe scale. For the skull itself, I'm planning a low-poly cranium with a tapering snout, nostrils, angled brow ridges, glowing teal eye sockets set in dark hollows, outward-sweeping ridged horns in an ivory tone, small jaw spikes, and a separate slightly-open lower jaw with teeth.

I'm adding upper teeth as merged cone rows plus fangs, and considering a simple rig with root, haft, head, and jaw joints so the jaw can hinge open for realism. I'm also thinking about adding a few small floating soul-wisp orbs near the blade for a LoL-style magical touch, shaped like teardrops with sphere bodies and tapering tails.

Now I'm deciding to make those wisps rise in a helical spiral around the haft, each with a glowing teal tail sweeping down to attach at the plinth so nothing feels truly detached. For the plinth itself I'm designing an octagonal tiered stone dais with a dark lathe base, an upper tier, a gold ring, and a glowing rune circle decal on top, plus small bone claw brackets.

Then I'm adding dragon-talon brackets gripping the haft base, teal crystal spikes around the plinth edge, and skipping the rib-arch cage idea since it would block the view. For the grip, I'm wrapping the haft in dark violet leather with diagonal spiral lines, capped by gold rings and a middle gem ring, then adding a hanging charm with a gold soul-chain detail.

I'm also placing a gold ferrule where the haft sinks into the plinth socket, a curling bone counter-spike shaped like a dragon claw near the blade root, and a jagged bone ridge of seven small spikes running along the blade's spine toward the tip.

I thought about adding serrated dragon-tooth notches to the cutting edge but decided to keep it smooth to avoid complicating the glowing edge strip. For the "soul window," I'm going with a smaller crescent inlay nested inside the blade, rendered as flat teal color since gradient paint won't support the glow effect.

I'm settling on a palette: bone ivory, bone shade, dark soulsteel, violet, teal glow, mint, gold, dark gold, leather, and stone for the plinth, keeping total colors under 64. Now I need to check how the glow tool and builder exports work so I can apply it to the soul channel strip and rune glyph overlay.

Since there are no sample directories to reference, I'm working from the builder documentation directly, checking signatures for joint and lathe parameters — lathe takes an axis and outline coordinates, and parts default to their nearest joint if none is specified. I'm planning a joint hierarchy: a root joint at the base, a haft joint above it aimed upward for most of the body, and a head joint as a child of the haft for the skull parts, with the plinth staying anchored to root.

Now I'm figuring out the skull's orientation (facing forward), where the jaw hinge sits, and where charm joints should attach relative to the head or collar. I'm also thinking about keeping the part count manageable by merging repeated small geometry rather than creating hundreds of individual pieces, and sketching a helper function to place parts with position, rotation, and a flat shading style for a low-poly look. For the bone material, I'm considering a mottled ivory paint with darker shading concentrated near the vertebra joints to suggest crevices between segments.

I want to compute that crevice darkening using the lathe's height parameter, finding the distance from either end and smoothly blending between a darker crevice tone and the base bone color near the ends. I'm checking whether paint functions can nest -- having one paint call into another paint's evaluation to combine effects, like layering a mottled texture with a shadow gradient. I also want a top-lit shading effect using a countershading technique between a lit bone tone and a shadowed one, driven by vertical position.

Now I'm working out the blade's outline shape -- defining the centerline radius and computing outer and inner half-width curves as functions of a parameter sweeping from the haft root to the tip, tapering the width down to a point while making the tip curve slightly asymmetric so the outer edge narrows faster than the inner edge for a more aggressive point.

I'm calculating actual coordinates: root starts around θ≈96-100° where x stays near 0 to avoid poking behind the haft, while the tip at θ=30° lands at roughly x=0.82, y=-0.425, giving a reasonable blade length of about 1.5 units relative to the haft.

Now I'm figuring out the blade's width profile, aiming for a bellied curve that's widest near the root and tapers out using a power function like (1-u)^0.75, then plotting outline points along that curve.

Then I'm working out the outline point sequence—tracing outer edge forward, inner edge back, marking sharp corners at tip and root, and making sure the tip isn't duplicated to avoid self-intersection. I'm also adding a thin highlight strip along the inner edge that tapers near the tip to suggest a sharpened bevel.

For the blade surface itself, I'm planning a dark steel base with a gradient overlay rendered as an SVG texture on a plane geometry sized to the blade's bounding box.

Mapping the blade shape into SVG coordinates, I'll draw filigree lines following the arc radius, small rune-like glyph marks, and dots, all in glowing teal strokes with transparency elsewhere so the texture reads as etched detail on the metal, keeping the bevel region small so the decoration sits on the flat face.

For the back face, since the plane faces the opposite direction, I need to generate a mirrored version of the SVG (flipping x) so the runes line up correctly with the blade geometry and still read properly from that side -- building a function that can produce both the normal and mirrored textures.

The texture plane gets positioned at the bounding box center in world coordinates. For the blade geometry, I'm setting up the main extrude with proper thickness and bevel along its local axes. Now I'm working out the spine bone ridge as a tapering capsule sweep along the outer edge, with periodic vertebra-like knobs.

Adding spike details along the bone and placing the ivory hub mount with gold collar rings and a glowing teal gem socket for the blade root.

Tapering the spike with a thin glow vein, then skipping the wing membrane idea to keep the silhouette focused on the blade and hook shapes. Now I'm moving to the skull details, placing the head joint and working out its coordinate frame in world space.

Figuring out how `bone` and `at` work together to position parts rigidly in model space. I'm laying out the skull itself—placing the cranium as an offset sphere tilted downward along the snout, positioned so the haft top passes behind it into the cranium, giving the effect of the skull mounted on the staff.

Mapping out the snout as a tapering frustum, the hinged lower jaw hanging open at an angle, rows of conical teeth with larger fangs, dark eye sockets holding small glowing orbs, angled brow ridges, nasal openings at the tip, and now starting to sweep out the horns.

I'm checking whether the horn tips as they curve up and outward might collide with the shoulder blade mount, since the geometry puts a horn point right around where the blade's top edge sits -- so I may need to raise the blade's root position to avoid the clash.

Let me reposition instead: lower the skull center, raise the vertebrae neck bone connecting to the blade hub, and sweep the horns mostly backward with only a slight outward curve so the tips land clear of the blade, while adding small frill fins along the jaw sides for extra silhouette detail.

Now I'm sketching the cheek frills as triangular spiked fans extruded sideways from the jaw, thin teal membranes with bone ribs, defining the outline in the base plane before adding thickness.

Still defining frill outline points...

I'll need to visually verify the spikes don't self-cross once rendered. Moving on to vertical placement, with the skull positioned around y=1.62.

I'm picturing how the haft relates to the skull in depth: if the skull faces forward and the haft sits behind it at the neck, the composition reads like the staff rising behind a perched skull. I'm weighing whether the haft should pass through the skull's jaws instead, so it looks like the skull is biting/gripping the staff rather than just sitting beside it awkwardly.

Settling on: skull snout angled down at roughly 35°, like a dragon head biting downward, with the haft entering the back of the skull at the occiput and vertebrae curving up into it. From the crown of the skull, a short bone post with vertebrae and a collar rises to meet the blade's hub, so the blade reads as emerging from the top of the skull rather than floating beside it.

I'm now nailing down a single consistent axis: haft runs vertically through x=0,z=0 from about y=0.14 up to 1.98, with the skull mounted around y=1.52–1.78 and the axis passing through its occiput. The haft itself is broken into vertebra sections — a lower run of seven vertebrae, then a leather-wrapped grip section above that — before transitioning into the skull mount.

Above the skull come two smaller post vertebrae and a hub around y=1.94–2.02, leading into the blade whose center sits near y=1.99. Total height comes out to roughly 2.2 meters including horn tips, with overall width around 1.2 meters, so I'm sizing the base plinth with tiered octagonal layers and a chamfered top disc with an inset glow ring, planning a mottled stone paint treatment for it.

Now I'm working on the rune circle plane near the haft socket, orienting it to face upward so the carved glyph texture reads correctly from the front, with concentric rings and tick marks forming a six-point star pattern generated via a small script. I'm also laying out six soul wisps in a helical arrangement around the lower haft, spaced 60 degrees apart at increasing heights up toward where they'd float just below the skull.

For the wisp tails, I'm building a tapering spiral path with a catmull curve from a thin point near the plinth ring up to the glowing head sphere, using a sweep radius that thickens from a sharp tip to match the head's size with a rounded cap. I'm giving each wisp head small dark eye details positioned slightly forward and up from center to suggest a tiny ghostly face, since they'll roughly face forward.

Now I'm thinking through colors -- a bright teal outer glow with a mint core -- and considering a hanging soul-lantern charm off the haft below the skull, with a gold ring anchor, a cord looping down with a teal crystal and tassels, positioned so it overlaps slightly with the haft without clashing with the wisps circling around it.

Writing grip wrap styling...

Working out texel density across the painted area—roughly 1.5 m² total for blade, plinth and other parts—gives around 1.4mm resolution at 1024px, so I'm considering bumping the atlas to 2048 or even 4096 to keep fine hand-painted details on things like the bone vertebrae crisp.

I'm laying out each vertebra as a faceted 8-segment lathe with ivory paint, then adding neural spine spikes angled forward-up along the front face to create the dragon's dorsal ridge.

For 13 vertebrae I'll just build individual lathe and cone parts rather than merging geometries, giving roughly 65 total pieces, and skip ribs to keep things simpler. I'm also adding a dark soulsteel core rod running underneath the vertebrae.

Between each vertebra I'll leave a small 0.012 gap and fill it with a thin glowing teal disc, like a cartilage joint seam, sized slightly smaller than the vertebra's end rim for a glowing-spine effect. Next I'm planning gold ferrules, grip rings, and collars via lathe outlines, plus figuring out how to apply the bone-mottle paint to the cranium sphere using its surface positions.

For the skull face, I'm adding a small glowing teal eye sphere with a dark socket and slanted brow-ridge boxes for an angry look, plus two tapered teal "ghost flame" wisps sweeping back from the eye sockets toward the frills. Then I'll add rows of small white tooth cones along the snout sides with two larger fangs, and start on a dorsal crest of small spikes along the top of the skull.

Now I'm thinking about adding floating "soul" elements near the blade: a few scattered loose octahedron shards drifting below the blade curve, plus a larger glowing mint soul orb with two thin tilted gold torus rings orbiting it, positioned in the concave inner curve of the blade near coordinates around (0.35-0.4, 1.55-1.78, 0).

I'm checking that this orb position sits safely inside the concave radius without clipping the blade edge, leaving a comfortable gap. I'm also considering adding tiny dark eye-like details inside the orb for a ghostly touch, and tethering it to the blade with a thin glowing teal wisp so it doesn't feel like an unattached loose part, echoing similar tendrils rising from the plinth toward the skull.

I'm shifting the orb outward to avoid colliding with the skull's frill tips, verifying the new position still stays within the inner curve radius with room to spare, and confirming the blade tip width leaves enough clearance. Now I'm setting up the imports and helper modules for the build script...

Defining the color palette...

Writing the bone paint shader with mottling and countershading effects...

Still refining crack logic...

Now I'm designing paint functions that accept the surface coordinate so I can shade vertebrae by height and blade geometry by radial distance from center, creating a spine ridge that fades toward the edges.

Writing blade shading function...

I need to double check the coordinate frame for the outline points -- the arc center C sits at (0, -0.9) in blade-local space, which lines up with the spine bone offset at (0, 1.99, 0) in world space. I'm defining a helper that converts an angle and radius into a world point using that combined offset.

Now I'm working out the blade profile parameters, with theta sweeping from 98° at the root to 30° at the tip, and width functions a(u) and b(u) tapering as a power curve. At the root the inner and outer radii create a nearly radial cut that the hub will hide, and at the tip both edges converge to a single sharp point.

Converting these polar coordinates to local x/y space, I sample 17 points along the outer edge and 16 along the inner edge to build the outline, then add a ridge sweep along the outer edge with a tapering radius for a bone-like spine effect, plus knobs and a gold trim band near the root.

I'm also planning tiny gold rivets along the blade spine and setting up the SVG viewBox and scale factors (mapping the meter-based bounding box into pixel coordinates) so I can draw a channel line that follows the blade's varying width between the inner and outer edges.

Now I'm defining helper offsets to draw two teal lines (one bright, one dim) that trace the blade's edge and spine curvature, plus a central rune line with eight glyphs spaced along the blade.

Each glyph is built from stroke templates sized relative to distance from the tip, placed using local tangent/normal vectors so they curve naturally with the blade. I'm adding dot accents, a diamond "soul-eye" motif near the hilt, and setting the whole overlay color scheme to teal with a mint highlight and a glow effect, plus a mirrored version for the back face.

Now I'm designing the plinth rune circle as its own SVG: concentric circles, tick-mark glyphs around the rim, and an inner hexagram made of two overlapping triangles, all in the same teal glow style. I'm also figuring out placement of the plane geometry on top of the plinth disc and confirming the haft and plinth parts all attach to the root bone correctly.

Then I'm defining the bone hierarchy: a haft joint positioned above the root, with the skull head bone as a child of the haft and the jaw bone as a child of the head. I'm working out the jaw hinge pivot point and how to pose it open by roughly 14 degrees, figuring out the correct rotation axis and sign convention so a forward-aimed jaw bone tips downward to open rather than closed.

Instead of applying a rotation pose, I decide it's simpler to just build the jaw geometry directly in its already-open position using a helper function that converts jaw-local coordinates (forward distance and vertical offset) into world space based on the hinge angle, then use that to place the lower jaw frustum boxes.

For the skull, I'm setting up similar local-axis logic with a tilt angle for the snout, positioning the upper snout frustum and cranium sphere relative to a defined origin point.

I want the skull to feel chunkier and more exaggerated relative to the blade, so I'm scaling up the snout length and skull width with a multiplier, then explicitly defining the dimensions and origin for the head geometry including brow ridges, eye sockets, frills, and cheek spikes.

Now I'm working through the cranium geometry — sizing the sphere radii for width, height, and depth, then setting up the forward tilt rotation so the snout angles downward correctly. From there I'm building the upper snout as a tapered frustum shape with its own position and radius transitions.

Working out nostril bulges and holes next, then the brow ridge — deciding whether to use rotated boxes or small cylindrical rods swept between points, picking segment counts for the rod cross-sections to keep things low-poly but still rounded enough.

Then I'm placing the eye sockets as recessed dark spheres with a slightly protruding glowing sphere poking through to read as an eye from the front, adjusting offsets so it sits naturally in the cranium surface. After that I start sketching the horn geometry as a bezier sweep curving back and outward from the crown of the skull.

Writing membrane coloring logic...

Checking the collision region more carefully, the blade's inner edge near x=0.35 sits around y≈1.81, while the frill's top edge at x=0.3 comes out to about 1.8 — so they're nearly touching right at that boundary, which seems like an acceptable overlap.

Working through the skull positioning, I'm adjusting the center down slightly to y=1.62, which repositions the neck post between the skull top (1.74) and hub (1.96), and lengthens the vertebrae chain down to 1.45. Laying out the grip from 0.74–1.12, upper vertebrae in four segments from 1.14–1.46, skull center at (0,1.60,0.04), post running 1.74→1.94, and hub spanning 1.94–2.04 with BY=1.99 — though I notice the cranium sphere top comes out to 1.73 with the 0.03 offset, so I need to double-check where the post actually starts from.

Now I'm designing the hub assembly: a bone block with gold plates on front and back, a glowing teal octahedron gem on each side, and making sure the hub's z-thickness comfortably exceeds the blade's thickness so the blade can pass through cleanly. I'm also sketching out a counter-spike on the back of the hub as a flattened, crescent-shaped extrusion that curves backward and upward to visually balance the blade.

That's fine. Skipping extra finger-bone details on the wing. For the plinth, I'll add three curling talon claws sweeping up from the base of the haft with a bezier curve.

Now I'm positioning them at 60°, 180°, and 300° so none obscure the front, adding a gold ferrule ring at the haft base, plus four teal crystal cones glowing at the plinth corners.

I'm adding stone scale texturing to the tier paint, a thin gold inlay ring, and eight outward-pointing ivory claw spikes around tier1's edge. Then I'm scattering ground clutter around the plinth base -- rib bone fragments, pebbles, and a few glowing teal shards resting at floor level.

Now I'm working out the plinth's lathe profile as an octagon, defining the radius and height coordinates for each tier's outline.

Writing lathe coordinates...

I'm reworking the tier3 radius and gold ring placement so the inlay fits properly within the tier boundary, then positioning the rune circle plane inside the ring's interior radius.

Now I'm sketching the ferrule collar where the haft meets the plinth, considering a gold ring with beveled edges and possibly a ribbon decoration lower on the haft.

Starting the actual build script now -- defining metadata, helper vectors, and setting up the joint hierarchy (root, haft, head, jaw) with their positions and parent relationships.

Since the path has 4 points making 3 spans, I need 4 names to include a tip, so I'll go with ["charm1","charm2","charm3","charmTip"]. Now I'm checking whether the charm's position overlaps with the haft's grip radius, since it hangs just in front of it.

I'm writing a vertebra-generation function that lathes a bone-like profile with a slight bulge at the midpoint, alternating spin angles for variety, making sure the outline stays non-negative in x and closes properly along the axis.

Now I'm planning the spine spikes: front spikes jutting toward +Z, transverse spikes splaying sideways with alternating length by index, and back spikes angled up and backward, giving roughly 13 vertebrae times 5 spikes each for about 65 parts total.

I'm sketching teal glow discs between each vertebra as thin lathed rings, then laying out the lower and upper spine sections with different pitches and tapering radii, and adding a dark inner haft rod running through the full length.

For the grip section I'm wrapping it in leather with gold collar rings at the top and bottom edges plus a decorative middle ring, each collar lathed with a beveled profile and small teal gem accents, then filling the gap above the grip with a glow disc before continuing the vertebra pattern further up the shaft.

Continuing up, I'm adding another gold collar and the hub section where the blade root attaches, then realizing the haft's vertebra segments need to account for the skull covering part of the axis — so I'm adding hidden, slightly larger vertebrae behind the skull to keep the structure continuous before resuming the visible post segments higher up.

Now I'm defining the skull's placement using an origin point and tilt angle, setting up helper vectors for forward/up directions to position the cranium relative to the neck axis.

I'm shaping the cranium with a scaled sphere geometry rotated to match the tilt, then adding the snout, back spurs, and jaw pivot with its own opening angle offset from the skull tilt.

Now I'm figuring out the lower jaw as a tapered frustum box between two jaw-space points, and planning the teeth as rows of small cones positioned along the snout's width, which narrows as it goes forward.

Still defining widths and tooth placement...

I'm reconsidering the eye trail paths so they don't collide with the horns -- curving them forward and upward from the eyes like flame shapes instead of sweeping along the skull.

I'll shorten the flame wisp to end around y=1.84, and leave the horn tips flared outward. Now I'm ready to move into writing the full code, including the blade overlay geometry and optional gold trim accents on the skull.

Adding gold horn rings...

I'll write a helper function to place bands along the path at given parameters, pulling radius from my taper function to keep things simple. For the charm, I'm sketching a basic teardrop-shaped SVG tassel with colored strands, and sizing the cards with a slight lean based on the reference doc.

Now I'm working out the hanging cards' orientation—frames facing up with a 180° lean—plus the cord chain, gem, and tassels attached near the charm tip with small positional offsets.

I'm also placing floating glowing shards around the blade, scattering a few small octahedrons at varied positions and rotations near the tip, then writing a loop to generate wisp paths with angular offsets and curving height profiles around a central radius.

The wisp path curves from a tail near the plinth up to a glowing sphere head, with a tapered radius sweep and a round sphere cap; I'm adding small dark eye spheres facing outward from the head plus a tiny mouth, all rendered with a teal-to-mint glow gradient along the tail to head. Now I'm setting up the orb—a glowing mint sphere with gold torus rings around it.

Adding a soul face with dark almond eyes and a mouth to the orb, plus a tether rod of small glowing beads connecting it up to a computed point on the blade's inner edge. I'm calculating the arc coordinates for that attachment point and spacing the beads along a slightly wobbly path, then moving on to texture the plinth stone with layered dark and light stone color variation.

I'm checking that the plinth sits flush on the floor and adding floor clutter like bone capsules lying flat, then reviewing what decal and paint layers I've already applied across the blade, plinth, haft, and frills to see if a cracked skull paint with glowing teal fractures is worth adding before finalizing. I still need to verify the correct option names for lathe, sweep, and part builder calls—things like sides, texture, and flat—so I'm planning to check the source types for those before writing the final code.

input.command: cd ~/tmp-archive/sonnet-100/soulScytheSonnet/ && grep -n "sides\|ngon\|flat?" src/sweep.ts | head -20; grep -n "export" src/math.ts | head -20; sed -n 1,60p kits/glow.ts; grep -n "texture\|flat" src/parts.ts | head -20
